title: Can Lifestraw save the world?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the LifeStraw water filter, the global lack of clean drinking water, and the diseases it causes. They cover waterborne illness deaths, guinea worm (dracunculus) and its eradication effort with the Carter Center, the original personal pipe filter and the LifeStraw Personal and LifeStraw Family filtration stages, and the filter's limits against Giardia, cryptosporidium, fluoride, heavy metals and arsenic. They discuss Vestergaard Frandsen's history, its relief products, the Rotary Club and Coca-Cola/Water for All partnership, and donation options. The episode closes with listener mail about the drug modafinil (misspoken as madafanel) and its addiction potential and medical use.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter, including a joke about an Olivia Newton John concert and a sponsor line for the reinvented 2012 camera.

segments.title: Global water access and the United Nations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the UN goal to halve the number of people lacking ready access to clean water, the roughly 1.1 billion people lacking access as of 2006, and how water scarcity holds back development.

segments.title: Waterborne disease and diarrhea deaths
segments.summary: They cite statistics that about six thousand people a day die from waterborne illness, and discuss how diarrhea, dehydration, malnutrition and HIV combine to cause deaths. They dispute the article's figure of 1.8 million diarrhea deaths, citing Giardia and cryptosporidium as major causes.

segments.title: Guinea worm and the origin of LifeStraw
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Vestergaard Frandsen company, which moved from textiles to relief products, and how Torben Vestergaard Frandsen developed the LifeStraw in 2005 to help fight guinea worm. The guinea worm life cycle and its spread through water are explained, and the original personal pipe filter is described as large.

segments.title: How the LifeStraw filter works and its family model
segments.summary: The personal LifeStraw is about ten inches long and filters roughly 700 liters over a year. Its stages are a coarse filter, a polyester filter down to about 15 microns, iodine-coated resin beads, and a carbon filter. The LifeStraw Family uses gravity, has a bucket, several filter stages, a chlorine chamber and ultrafiltration, can be backflushed, and filters about 18,000 liters over three years.

segments.title: Limits of LifeStraw and the multi-pronged approach
segments.summary: The personal LifeStraw cannot remove Giardia (which resists iodine), cryptosporidium, fluoride, heavy metals or arsenic. The family model does filter Giardia and cryptosporidium. Water Aid's Paul Heatherington is cited on education and wells as the real solution, with LifeStraw as a stopgap.

segments.title: Donations, corporate partnerships and ethics
segments.summary: The hosts discuss costs (about three to six dollars per unit, six fifty via Rotary) and the ethics of combining capitalism with relief. They describe the Coca-Cola and Water for All partnership that donated 27,000 LifeStraws to Africa, and other donation routes including the Carter Center, the Project H Design hippo roller, and Vestergaard's malaria nets and HIV care packs.

segments.title: Guinea worm eradication and water conservation
segments.summary: The hosts note that guinea worm is near eradication and would be only the second human disease eradicated after polio. Chuck encourages water conservation, recalling Atlanta's drought restrictions and reusing water.

segments.title: Listener mail on modafinil
segments.summary: Listeners correct the hosts' pronunciation of modafinil and discuss its use. A neurobiology PhD student notes its trials for cocaine addiction and that non-dopamine effects can still be addictive. Another listener says it has helped his sleep disorder and that doctors prescribe it for medical conditions.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners for expert feedback, give the show email, and close with a sponsor line.
